title_en: Qu Cheng v. Kowloon Customs — dispute over administrative penalty decision

full_text_en:
Ou Cheng v. Kowloon Customs — administrative penalty dispute

Plaintiff: Ou Cheng, male, 69 years old, residing at Flat 4, 29th Floor, Hejian Court, Xiangheyuan, Kwun Tong, Kowloon, Hong Kong.

Defendant: Kowloon Customs of the People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Liu Wenjie, Commissioner of Kowloon Customs.

Agents ad litem: Zhou Weihang and Li Guo, both officers of Kowloon Customs.

Plaintiff Ou Cheng, dissatisfied with the reconsideration decision on the penalty made by Kowloon Customs of the People's Republic of China, filed a lawsuit with the Intermediate People's Court of Shenzhen, Guangdong Province. The court lawfully formed a collegial panel and held a public hearing, finding that:

Plaintiff Ou Cheng, when entering China through Luohu Customs on December 4, 1987, did not carry any jade articles. On December 6, the plaintiff carried 317 pieces of jade articles, placed in his luggage, without declaring them to customs. When departing through the "green channel" (i.e., the channel for items not requiring declaration) at Luohu Port, he was intercepted when passing through the baggage inspection machine. Upon appraisal by the Guangdong Provincial Cultural Relics Administration, among the jade articles carried by the plaintiff, one piece was a jade dragon belt hook, which was a cultural relic from the early Qing Dynasty and prohibited for export; two pieces (one jade belt hook and one white jade monkey) were cultural relics from the late Qing Dynasty; the remaining 314 pieces were various modern special jade craft products. The estimated total value of these jade articles was RMB 9,580.

On February 27, 1988, Luohu Customs issued a penalty decision, finding that Ou Cheng violated the provision of Article 29, Paragraph 1 of the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that "All owners of inward and outward articles shall make a truthful declaration to the Customs and be liable to Customs examination." According to Article 3, Item (2) of the Rules for the Implementation of Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China, Ou Cheng, passing through a place where Customs is established, used concealment, disguise, and false declaration to evade customs supervision, carried articles prohibited for export by the state, passed through the "green channel" when departing, and the quantity and value of the articles carried far exceeded the limits prescribed by the state in the "List of Duty-Free and Dutiable Articles Limits for Passengers Traveling between Hong Kong, Macau, and the Mainland", thus constituting smuggling. In accordance with Article 5, Item (2) of the Rules for the Implementation of Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law, it was decided to impose a penalty of confiscation of all the jade articles carried.

The plaintiff, dissatisfied with the penalty decision of Luohu Customs, applied to Kowloon Customs for reconsideration on March 3, 1988. Upon reconsideration, Kowloon Customs held that the penalty decision of Luohu Customs against Ou Cheng was appropriate, that the grounds for reconsideration were untenable, and decided to uphold the original penalty decision.

The plaintiff, dissatisfied with the reconsideration decision of Kowloon Customs, on the grounds that the jade articles he carried were all craft products, not unearthed cultural relics or jadeite jade, but craft products carved from mountain stone, and should be allowed for export, and that Luohu Customs improperly confiscated these articles, filed a lawsuit with the Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court on July 1, 1988, requesting the protection of his lawful rights and interests and the return of the confiscated articles.

The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court, upon trial, held that: When Plaintiff Ou Cheng departed for Hong Kong, the articles he carried included cultural relics prohibited for export by the state and special jade craft products subject to quantitative restrictions on export by the state, not craft products carved from mountain stone. Furthermore, he mixed them in his luggage, failed to declare them to customs, and was intercepted when choosing to pass through the green channel. His conduct violated Article 29, Paragraph 1 and Article 48 of the Customs Law and constituted smuggling. The defendant, Kowloon Customs, made the reconsideration decision to confiscate the jade articles carried by the plaintiff in accordance with Article 3, Item (2) and Article 5, Item (2) of the Rules for the Implementation of Administrative Penalties under the Customs Law, and that decision was correct.

In summary, on November 15, 1988, the court rendered the following judgment:

Affirmed the reconsideration decision of Kowloon Customs to confiscate the jade articles of Plaintiff Ou Cheng.

The litigation costs of this case, HKD 200, shall be borne by the plaintiff.
